subtopic: YOUTH TRAINING PROGRAM
YOUTH TRAINING PROGRAM
speechtext:
1.	What opportunities are being offered to rural youth under the dominion-provincial youth training program?
2.	Which provinces have to date signified their intention of continuing the youth training program under the dominion-provincial arrangement of last year?

subtopic: YOUTH TRAINING PROGRAM
speechtext:
1.	The following courses are available to rural youth under the dominion-provincial youth training program:

Prince Edward Island-
Courses for young women in homecraft and cooking, home nursing, first aid, handicrafts.
Courses for young men in blacksmithing, carpentry, farm mechanics and general agricultural subjects, fishing (including simple accounting, curing, boning, packing and marketing of fish)-forestry (cultivation and care of woodlots), rural leadership courses at St. Francis Xavier University.
Nova Scotia-
Courses for young women in cooking, homecraft, handicrafts, home nursing, beekeeping, poultry, gardening.
Courses for young men in egg and poultry grading, farm mechanics, short agricultural courses in specialized subjects.
New Brunswick-
Courses for young women in homecraft and handicrafts.
Courses for young men in rural leadership at St. Francis Xavier University, courses in agriculture at Carleton county school and Fredericton Agricultural College, forestry training during summer of 1937.
Quebec

Courses for young women in homecraft, handicrafts and agricultural subjects in parishes.
Courses for young men in forestry training during winter-agricultural cooperatives and training for credit unions-two-week parish courses in agricultural subjects.
Ontario-
Courses for young women in catering (two-week courses) for tourists, rug weaving, dressmaking and sale of home-baked products.
Manitoba-
Courses for young women lasting six weeks to three months in agricultural subjects, home-

Questions
craft, handicrafts, dressmaking, physical education and citizenship with provision for recreation, dramatics, etc.
Courses for young men group taking six months course in agriculture at the the University of Manitoba.
Courses six weeks to three months in agricultural subjects with provision for recreation and social activities.
Saskatchewan-
Courses for young women lasting from one week to six weeks in agricultural subjects, homecraft, home nursing, handicrafts and dressmaking, recreation, etc.
Courses for young men lasting two weeks to two months in general and specialized agricultural subjects, farm mechanics and management, also attendance at short and long winter agricultural courses at the University of Saskatchewan directed by the extension department of the University of Saskatchewan.
Alberta-
Provision has been made for farmers' sons to attend the six months courses at the agricultural schools at Olds and Vermilion.
Courses for both young men and young women lasting two to four weeks with provision for separate class instruction and practical demonstrations in agricultural subjects, farm mechanics, farm management and accounting, poultry, etc. Homecraft and handicraft, citizenship and general cultural subjects. Provision for recreation, evening programs, debates, etc.
British Columbia-
One course in chick sexing.
The total number of young people participating in the courses enumerated above is approximately 10,000.
2.	The provinces of British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island have signified their intention to continue the youth training program along the general lines of the present agreements. Ontario has definitely stated its intention to continue home service training, and is still giving consideration to the balance of the training items at present in operation.

speechtext: That when this house adjourns on Wednesday, 13th of April, it stand adjourned until Monday, 25th April, 1938 (daylight saving time).

subtopic: EASTER ADJOURNMENT FROM FRIDAY, APRIL 8, UNTIL MONDAY, APRIL 25
speechtext: I desire to suggest to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that he change the motion to read " 8th of April " instead of " 13th of April." As a westerner, and I believe many other western members will agree, I think it would be advisable to have a few more days. The additional Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday, Wednesday being the short day of the week, might facilitate the closing of business at an earlier date after Easter. I hope the Prime Minister will consider this proposed change.

subtopic: EASTER ADJOURNMENT FROM FRIDAY, APRIL 8, UNTIL MONDAY, APRIL 25
speechtext: I concur in what has been said by the previous speaker (Mr. Perley). If the house were to adjourn on the Friday previous to April 13 I do not believe it would prolong the session, and, by giving them practically an additional five days, it would give hon. members who live at a distance from Ottawa, whether east or west, an opportunity of visiting their homes or their constituents. If the present motion is adhered to and we adjourn on Wednesday, April 13, quite a number of members will be absent during those three days. Under these circumstances, and in view of the probability of the session being shorter than was at first expected, I support the change suggested by the hon, member for Qu'Appelle.

subtopic: EASTER ADJOURNMENT FROM FRIDAY, APRIL 8, UNTIL MONDAY, APRIL 25

speechtext:
What matter?
Hon. NORMAN McL. ROGERS (Minister of Labour): The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) was good enough to give me notice of his intention to ask this question this afternoon. I did receive a telegram from the acting mayor of Vancouver directing attention to the relief situation in that city and suggesting it was desirable that the government should come to its financial assistance. In reply to that telegram I advised the acting mayor of Vancouver that the dominion government pays a grant in aid direct to the province of British Columbia; it does not control and has never controlled the financial arrangements between the provincial government and its municipalities. I also advised the acting mayor that at the moment the dominion is carrying out to the letter its commitments, as contained in several formal agreements under the present relief legislation, entered into with the province after very careful study of the various problems confronting the province of British Columbia.
My hon. friend has asked me what we are prepared to do to meet the situation in that province. May I inform him of what we are doing at the present time in that connection. During the present fiscal year, which will end on March 31, the dominion government will have contributed to the province of British Columbia as a grant in respect to material aid, that is, for the
Unemployment Insurance

provision of the necessities of life-food, fuel, clothing and shelter-to those in need, the sum of $1,500,000. In addition to this the dominion government has, under the agreement of June 11, 1937, agreed to contribute fifty per cent of the cost of a program of provincial and municipal works to relieve unemployment, the dominion contribution amounting to approximately $522,000.
In addition, under the youth training agreement, the dominion government has agreed to contribute $100,000 to match a like sum to be expended by the province in carrying out training projects for unemployed young people, and under this plan, at the end of February, 8,580 youths were receiving assistance.
The farm improvement and employment plan in effect in the western provinces is not so well suited to the conditions in British Columbia as it is to other western provinces, and under this plan only 270 placements have been made. However, a supplementary plan of forest development and improvement works for transients has provided for a contribution from the federal government which will amount to an expenditure of approximately $500,000.
All these plans are covered by agreement between the federal government and the province, including the grant in respect to material aid; but it will be understood that the material aid agreement, while providing for a monthly payment to the province, does not and cannot provide as to the amount which the province shall transfer or allot to any particular municipality or district. This is, and must be, a matter to be decided by the provincial authorities, and it is for this reason that the mayor of Vancouver has been advised that the dominion government makes the grant directly to the province, but does not control financial arrangements between the provincial governments and the municipalities.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO INTENTION TO PROCEED WITH LEGISLATION AT THE PRESENT SESSION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO INTENTION TO PROCEED WITH LEGISLATION AT THE PRESENT SESSION
speechtext: May I ask the Prime Minister whether it is the intention of the government to proceed at this session with legislation dealing with the question of unemployment insurance?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO INTENTION TO PROCEED WITH LEGISLATION AT THE PRESENT SESSION
speechtext:
My hon. friend gave me an intimation of his intention to ask the

question he has just asked. I believe I can best answer it by outlining what thus far has been done in the present situation.
The proposal to the provinces that they agree to an -amendment to the British North America Act to enable parliament to enact unemployment insurance legislation, was made on November 5 last. As the house is already aware, six of the provinces, British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario, Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia, accepted the proposal at that time. The premiers of Alberta and New Brunswick, after some exchange of correspondence, indicated their intention to submit the proposed amendment to the provincial legislatures for their consideration. The premier of Quebec agreed as to the desirability of unemployment insurance, but suggested that it might be instituted by concurrent legislation.
On January 20, the draft of the proposed amendment was submitted to the provinces. Five of them, British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia, expressed approval of its terms. This communication has not been acknowledged by the premier of Ontario. Approval by the government of Ontario of the proposal to amend the British North America Act was, however, set forth in Mr. Hepburn's letter of November 25, in the following terms:
Following a cabinet council meeting of yesterday's date, I am pleased to inform you that the government of the province of Ontario is prepared to waive any constitutional objections and to give the fullest measure of cooperation and support to the proposed amendments to the British North America Act, empowering the federal government to enact unemployment insurance legislation.
The premier of Quebec has not, thus far, acknowledged the draft amendment. The premier of Alberta, in a letter dated March 15, stated that it was his intention to have the matter taken up before the Alberta legislature in the immediate future. The premier of New Brunswick has not yet acknowledged the communication of January 20, but the proposal was referred to in the speech from the throne delivered at the opening of the New Brunswick legislature on February 24, in the following terms:
Consistent with their conception of the constitution and the principles of responsible government, my ministers, without discussing the merits of the proposal, took the position that the question should be determined by the legislature and the federal government was so advised.
The speech from the throne at the opening of the present session of parliament contained the following statement:

Seed Grain
The cooperation of the provinces has been sought with a view to an amendment of the British North America Act, which would empower the parliament of Canada to enact forthwith a national scheme of unemployment insurance. My ministers hope the proposal may meet with early approval, in order that unemployment insurance legislation may be enacted during the present session of parliament.
In the circumstances, to which I have referred, the government do not feel it would be desirable to make a further statement before the remaining provinces have had an opportunity of indicating their views.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES

speechtext:
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 78, to assist the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan in financing the cost of seed and seeding operations for the crop year 1938.
Mr. E.	E. PERLEY	(Qu'Appelle):	Wehave now before us the bill in printed form, and while it deals in a general way with the dominion's guarantee and the terms of that guarantee to the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, I do not think that there is sufficient	information	in	detail	in the	billitself. I	desire now,	therefore,	to ask	for
some more information, and I propose to discuss the bill from three important angles.
In the	first place	I	should	like to	be
assured by the minister that provision will be made, either in the bill itself or in the regulations governing the distribution of seed, to see that every farmer has a reasonable amount of seed in order that he may seed a fair average number of acres under cultivation; in other words, that each farmer who has a summer fallow in a sufficiently good state of cultivation #to be seeded be provided with that seed. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) the other evening in discussing this matter, said that possibly some arrangement would be made with the banks or the mortgage companies
with a view to assisting the farmer, but I should like to have some definite provision made to make sure of that.
The second angle from which I propose to discuss the bill is the price to the farmer.
I think we should make sure that the price will not be unjust, that it will not be too high. This is necessary for the protection not only of the farmer but of the taxpayer if the guarantee ever has to be met.
In the third place, I think provision should be made to provide power to seed the crop in proper season.
With respect to the first point, judging by the regulations that have been issued to the municipalities by the Minister of Agriculture in Saskatchewan, I suggest that there will not be sufficient seed supplied to many of the farmers who have a section or two of land, and I trust that something 'will be done in that respect. I want to know how the minister arrives at the price of SI .40 to $1.45. In the regulation issued by the Department of Agriculture in Regina it is stated that the price to the farmer will be $1.45 or thereabouts. The Minister of Finance said on Friday that the price should be an average price.
While I am on my feet, I propose to ask a few questions. It is very unsatisfactory in asking questions to have other hon. members intervene before the minister has replied to them all, so that one does not get a consecutive series of questions and answers. I shall endeavour to put my questions so that the minister will know what information I am seeking.
I think we should know in what future the 6,964,000 bushels was held as at August 1, 1937, and the price of that option. We have here to-day at least three members of the cabinet who are members of an advisory committee to the wheat board representing the government. I hold in my hand a report issued by the Canadian Wheat Board, dated January 6, 1938. On page 1 of that report I find two paragraphs which I am going to read:
Our unsold wheat at 31st July, 1937, amounted to 6,964,000 bushels, represented by futures contracts, which in the ordinary course of business would have been disposed of prior to that date.
Towards the latter part of the crop season it was apparent that western Canada was again faced with a very small crop; in the province of Saskatchewan, particularly, conditions were disastrous and it was obvious that seed wheat would be required over a very large area. After consultation with the wheat committee of the cabinet it was considered expedient to retain the futures contracts referred to in order to exchange them for cash wheat suitable for seed requirements in that
Seed Grain

province. By arrangement with the government of the province of Saskatchewan the wheat thus accumulated has been sold to them.
I might also mention that I have here order in council P.C. 3113, passed on December 15, which relates to this matter, and I desire to put it on the record. It is as follows:
The committee of the privy council have had before them a report, dated 13th December, 1937, from the Minister of Trade and Commerce, stating that the Canadian wheat' board advise with regard to the question of converting wheat futures into actual wheat to be used for seed and feed relief in the province of Saskatchewan, that arrangements have been made by the Saskatchewan government for the purpose of this wheat, and that all charges in connection with the handling, such as premiums, storage, transportation and any additional charges will be paid by the Saskatchewan government.
The minister, therefore, recommends that the Canadian Wheat Board be authorized to exchange the long futures contracts that they have on hand as at July 31, 1937, namely 6,964,000 bushels, for actual wheat to be used for seed and feed purposes in the province of Saskatchewan in connection with the sowing of the 1938 crop.
The committee concur in the foregoing recommendation and submit the same for approval.
That order in council is the first authority that was issued to the board to convert the options. The spread or premium on the cash wheat between the option and the cash, from August 31 to December 15 when that order in council was passed, widened from 6 to 27 cents. I think we should know why this premium widened on wheat in the interior elevators. Possibly the grain trade had some idea of the conversion that was likely to take place in December and prepared to make another little rake-off from the board. There was no special export demand to warrant a premium at that time, as I shall show from figures I have from the bureau of statistics. And wheat in the interior elevators was not in a position to command a premium. The Minister of Finance is an expert grain man. Before he entered political life he had very wide experience in managing one of the most successful grain organizations in western Canada, and he made a success of it. He knows that wheat in the interior of the western provinces does not command a premium as it might if it were at the terminals, where it would be available for immediate shipment in case an exporter were short on a cargo. If an exporter has chartered a vessel to ship grain and is a little short of a certain grade, wheat of that grade in another elevator would be at a premium to enable him to finish the cargo. But I ask the minister to explain why wheat in the elevators in the interior commanded the premium that it did over the option.

In dealing with the price the minister said he thought the average price from July 31 until the operations were concluded, or the day the provincial government took over the wheat, should prevail. I do not agree to that. I admit that you have to have some basis on which to start figuring your price, but I cannot agree that the price should be the cash price averaged between those dates.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: I did not say the cash price.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: Well, the minister said the average price from July 31 to the time the government of Saskatchewan takes it over.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: If my hon. friend will permit, there were two questions discussed. One was the average base price, and the other the premium.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: Does the minister agree that there should not be a premium?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: I am not qualified to say that. I do not know how you would get the wheat without it.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
I want to try to figure what I think the price of this wheat should be to the farmer. First, to the price of the option taken from the board as of December, 1935, when the new board took over, add the storage charged from the date the wheat was taken over by the province of Saskatchewan, or even by the board from the date of their conversion. That would be the storage on the grain as it was taken over following that conversion. Add to that the transportation, that is the cost of moving it from point to point within the province, and the cost of distribution. I consider that the most we could allow for storage would be say five cents. The storage rate at the terminals is one cent a month. For five months that would be five cents, which should be sufficient. While I am trying to figure out how I arrive at what the price should be, I should like to have the attention of the two ministers. I am allowing five cents for storage and ten cents for transportation from one point to another within the province. Then I am allowing three cents for the distribution costs, which I think should be ample. That is a total of eighteen cents. Then I consider that the price of the option as taken over by the new board would not be more than 90 cents, at the very most; I think it would be a little under that. That would give a figure of $1.08, or at the most $1.10, at which the wheat should be charged to the farmer.
The minister may be able to give some other explanation, but I am going to suggest to the house what I think would be the procedure in

Seed Grain
converting that wheat. The board would notify the clearing house that they were long in options, nearly 7,000,000 bushels of wheat, and that they desired to convert those options into cash wheat within the provinces. In other words they would notify the clearing house that they desired to take delivery of that wheat. Then it would be up to the clearing house to get that wheat, not necessarily within the provinces, but the clearing house certainly would have to get it at the point of delivery, which is at the terminal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: Tort William.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
Yes, Fort William. Then the wheat board, having taken over the wheat on the option at Fort William, could sell it there and buy wheat in the interior, or they could make an exchange. The minister smiles a little; perhaps he will be able to explain this away. I know he is an expert in the grain business, but the board will have wheat at the terminals, because that is the only place where- the board can call the options. I think the minister will agree with that. Having it there the board could either sell the wheat and buy cash wheat in the interior or make exchange arrangements with the elevator people. Therefore I claim that the wheat would cost the board exactly what the option cost. Of course the extra storage and transportation charges would have to be added, but I am dealing with the original cost.
The minister may say there were switching operations, and things of that sort. I have before me the report of the wheat board dated January 6, 1938, and I want to refer to page 3 in connection with the switching operations. This is what I find:
The expenses of the board during the year, covering all administration and operating expense together with storage on wheat carried, amounted to $330,567.69. This was, however, more than offset by revenue accruing from the switching of nearby future contracts into contracts for deferred months. This revenue, together with interest earned on funds on hand, amounted to $424,487.42, thus leaving a credit balance of $93,919.73 after meeting all the board's operating expenses in Canada.
According to this statement the board made money in their switching operations, and in that connection I take it that this dates back to December of 1935. They say they earned also some interest on funds which they deposited, no doubt with the banks.

speechtext: Two million dollars was deposited with the dominion government.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
I may point out also that they had no charge for margins; that is, no interest could be charged in connection with money on deposit with the clearing house,
since I have it on authority from the directors that the government was not asked to carry any margins on its account.
I wish to quote further from the evidence taken by the special committee, in order to show that the position of the wheat board was not affected by their switching operations, in order to indicate that the price at which we should figure this wheat is the original price of the option. I have before me the printed copy of the evidence taken before the special committee on the marketing of wheat and other grains, in 1936. At page 60 of this evidence we have a statement by Mr. Murray, in reply to questions put to him by myself, with respect to these switching operations:
By Mr. Perley:
Q. Do you not think it weakens your position when you go into the October?
That is, switching from the July to the October.
That is, the new crop month. Switches are made into July and then July into October.- A. No.
Q. They would have the new crop to deliver on those old contracts?-A. It does not weaken our position.
Further down I find this:
Q. But it is cleaning up your May and cleaning up your July, to get it into the October?-A. It does not weaken our position in any way. The only thing that would weaken our position, being placed as we are with the responsibility of selling wheat, would be to exchange one option for an option that was not so readily saleable.
So there is a statement by Mr. Murray that their position was not weakened, and I could read further from the next page, where he states what a corner he could have manipulated had he so desired, and then he would have been able to call the shorts and make them dance a nice tune. The point I desire to make is that in changing the options from one month to another right through from 1935 the position of the board has not been changed, and the price that should be attached to that wheat is whatever the option stood them when they took over in 1935, which is a little less than 90 cents.
I should like the minister to tell us who is making the difference in this spread, which widened from 6 to 27 cents between August 31 and December 15. I should like also to know the number of bushels converted each month. I think .this would be important, because then we could arrive at the storage fees that should be charged. If it was all converted during December or January it would make a considerable difference in the storage charges. Also I think we should know the position the wheat was in when the pro-
Seed Grain

vincial government took it over; that is, the position in the interior of these provinces. Then we could figure what the transportation costs might be. I think we should know also when the provincial governments assumed the whole responsibility. The wheat is going out now. If we should happen to hold up this measure for a day or two I do not think it would make any particular difference, because the wheat is going out. I have here a report in a newspaper which came to hand to-day, which says:
Seed wheat is being shipped. Movement of seed wheat and supplies is already under way to the first of 1,120 points in Saskatchewan, according to Hon. J. G. Taggart, provincial minister of agriculture. Of this number between 900 and 1,000 will receive wheat deliveries. The Canada grain board has already authorized the movement of 6,500,000 bushels of grain. All the wheat is 1937 wheat from prairie points.
So the wheat was grown in 1937 in the three prairie provinces. I say the wheat is going forward now, so if this measure is held up for a day or two it will not make very much difference, and I think the public are entitled to some of the information for which we are asking. At page 1695 of Hansard the Minister of Agriculture stated:
Yes, Mr. Chairman. As the Minister of Finance has just said, this matter has been under discussion for the last six months. In the first place it is necessary to secure sufficient quantities of the different types of grain to be used for seeding purposes. That is the first job to be done.
He said further:
But I must say that in both Saskatchewan and Alberta agreement was reached between this government and the two provincial governments as to the amount of guarantee required in each province.
That shows that it had been under consideration for a number of months. I think we should have the figures with respect to the acreage to be seeded and the amount of seed required. I should like to know how the amount of the guarantee was arrived at. How was the price per bushel arrived at? How did the government arrive at these figures without knowing the number of acres in each province to be seeded? There was a question on the order paper to-day with reference to the acreage under cultivation in the area requiring seeding. I think we should have this information, as well as the requirements for the purposes of sowing oats, wheat, barley, rye and flax.
I do not think the Minister of Finance or the Minister of Agriculture can expect the house to approve this bill in a short space of time without it having this information before

it. In connection with the amount of wheat in Saskatchewan, the minister made this statement, to be found on page 1702 of Hansard, in reply to a question by myself:
Between now and the time when the bill is down for second reading and in committee, every endeavour will be made to arrive definitely at a conclusion. The matter is a very difficult and complex one. My hon. friend in his last few sentences asks how much wheat the wheat board was holding on this account in Saskatchewan as of March 15. He knows they were able to acquire mighty little of this wheat in Saskatchewan. If they had any in that province at that time it would be because, having been acquired, this wheat in the process of physical movement had been moved that much nearer to its ultimate destination.
I have before me figures taken from the weekly reports of the grain commission in Winnipeg showing the amount of wheat on hand in the interior elevators, in the private elevators, in the mills and in the terminal elevators of the three provinces. For the week ending August 6, 1937, the total wheat In store was 7,284,211 bushels.

No, I have not. I have the amount of durum and the remainder is just northern wheats. There is a considerable amount of durum. It is interesting to note that since August 1 there has been a considerable amount of grain in store in these provinces, that is wheat grown in 1937. The minister asked if I had the grades, but I

Seed Grain
think he will agree with me when I say that a dry season such as we had last year, when there was no frost in the fall, tends to create high grades of wheat, generally speaking. If you follow these reports you will see that in the months of September, October and November there was considerable wheat shipped out of Saskatchewan, but then the elevators seem to have got up again to the previous average.
The Minister of Finance knows from his own experience that as soon as the heaviest runs of wheat are delivered to the interior elevators the elevator companies try to fill their elevators to carry the wheat over for the winter months. They like to store the wheat up to about May in order to get the carrying charges. This practice may account for some wheat being in that position. There is plenty of wheat in Saskatchewan to satisfy the requirements. I am concerned in the government seeing to it that the government of Saskatchewan guarantees or assists the municipalities in the providing of power to get the crops in at the proper time. The Minister of Agriculture is reported on page 1696 of Hansard as follows:
The other question raised, with regard to provision for live stock or for power in order to put in the crop, is not an immediate concern of this government.
That statement should not have been forthcoming from the minister. I think it should be the immediate concern of this government to see that there is sufficient power with which to put in a crop. A further statement by the minister, to be found on the same page of Hansard, is as follows:
The question whether or not horses have come back in poor shape is not one with which I can deal, other than to say that in all the cheeks I have been able to make-and I have been over quite a part of the area during the last few weeks-I have not found that great numbers of horses have died; I have not found that they are any poorer than they usually are after going through a year of this kind, in any part of the dominion. It is perfectly true that if you put a number of horses, cattle, or any other live stock into a boxcar and carry them three or four hundred miles probably you will have to take one of them home on a stone-boat, as the result of what they do to one another during the journey. You may even have to take one out that is not worth hauling home, but these stories are very much enlarged upon, and the checks we have been able to make indicate that the death rate among live stock this year is not materially greater than in any average year in western Canada.
I take exception to that statement, because I think the mortality among the horses has been considerably greater. While the minister may have had experts checking it, as he states, I think the authorities which I have
are just as reliable as some of his checkers.
I have received numerous letters from councillors of different municipalities and from reeves and reliable farmers. I know my own district pretty thoroughly; within a radius of forty or fifty miles of my own district we have lost at least thirty per cent of the horses this winter, and I think that is the average for the southern part of the province. Certainly fifty per cent of the horses that were there last fall are not ready to go to work. In any paper you pick up you will find some report to that effect. Here, for instance, is a snapshot of some horses that are described as typical examples of horses returning to Saskatchewan farms from the winter pasturage at Carberry. The minister can see the paper in the reading room. These horses are part of a carload that was brought back, and certainly they are in no condition to work within the next six weeks or two months. It would take a good many bushels of oats to put them to work, and the story in this paper is not very complimentary to the government.
I also read in to-day's papers coming forward from Saskatchewan that the Royal Humane Society in Moose Jaw and Regina are both of the opinion that some action should be taken to enforce the act with respect to cruelty to animals. Here is one dispatch:
Regina members of the Royal Humane Society and the Saskatchewan society for the prevention of cruelty to animals will approach the government to determine the exact condition of horses returned to southern Saskatchewan from government-sponsored pasturage.
It goes on to say that the Moose Jaw branch of the society is taking similar action.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a rather long way from Nova Scotia to the west, but I should like to say a few words on this bill.
This bill is for the direct benefit of a portion only of this great country, and while on general principles I am opposed to federal legislation that is not applicable to Canada as a whole, I agree that in view of the situation facing us in the west some such legislation as this is necessary. On general principles I am also opposed to federal guarantees, on the ground that if a condition is of sufficient importance or seriousness to warrant financial assistance, the government should advance the money at once instead of adopting the more expensive method now proposed to the house. It is only too well known that for some reason securities carrying a government guarantee are usually quoted at a lower rate than similar direct obligations of the government, thus making the money more expensive. In the present instance, however, realizing that- the chartered banks have the necessary machinery for handling the business which is lacking by the government, I wish to congratulate the government on this provision of the bill, particularly when it seems to be almost a foregone conclusion that when the federal government makes an advance in the district with which we are now dealing the money is lost to the federal treasury.
I do, however, question the rate of interest and would suggest to the government that they consider increasing it to something nearer the rate which private business has to pay, say 5 to 51 per cent, with the provision lhat on any advance which the federal treasury has to make good the rate will be reduced to 21 or 3 per cent. This would be a greater incentive to the banks to collect and would lighten the drain on the treasury.
Having discussed a few features of the bill from the federal standpoint, may I be per-

Seed Grain
mitted to discuss it for a few moments from a maritime province view? In this connection I cannot too strongly urge on the government favourable consideration of the very reasonable request of the hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacLean), made in this house on Friday last, with regard to seed grain for maritime farmers. I do not propose to approach this subject from the angle of the beam trawlers, nor yet from the angle of the dumping duty on sugar, but I do propose to discuss it from the viewpoint of 25,000 to 30.000 people in my constituency, who are, in whole or part, dependent on agriculture for their livelihood, and from the viewpoint of the half million people of the maritime provinces who are in the same category. A hardworking and industrious body of people, loyal to the British Empire, loyal to Canada and loyal to the little provinces down by the sea, they believe in thrift and do not make a practice of parading their ills before successive governments at Ottawa. To my mind they are the backbone not only of the maritime provinces but also of the dominion. I do not need to point out to this house the number of leaders in all walks of life in Canada and in the United States whose background is a farm in one of the maritime provinces.
These people are generous to a fault; a very large proportion of the contributions to the west last fall, already referred to by the hon. member for Prince, came from them. They are proud of being a part of Canada; for this reason they approach problems from a national standpoint, with, I think, the result that they have not in the past received the same consideration as their more vocal and, in my opinion, less deserving cousins in other parts of Canada. They do claim, however, that legislation should apply equally to them as to other parts of Canada, and for that reason they fail to see the justice of such imposts as the duty on corn, of which they buy a considerable quantity in their mixed farming operations. This duty is apparently only for the benefit of a small section of our country, already highly subsidized by tariffs on manufactured goods. The result of this duty has a direct bearing on the price of all feed, thus causing our maritime people to pay a further toll to the grain producers of the west, already heavily assisted by the government. I trust that the government will see to it that this and similar duties are removed or else duties imposed on such items as vegetable oils; because it is most unfair that they should be required to pay heavy duties on goods that enter into their production and be subject to open competition on the goods they produce. Here I should like to say it is to the undying credit of the 51952-111
present government that their trade policies have been quite beneficial to the farmers of the maritime provinces.
The west is not the only part of Canada where droughts occur. In 1934 the hay crop in Nova Scotia was almost a complete failure. There was no suggestion that the federal government pay for the hay and feed. That year hay cost our farmers 811 to $12 a ton in Quebec and Ontario, f.o.b. cars. The local government made arrangements for the farmers to obtain a reduction of two-t'hirds of the freight, leaving a net cost to our people of $14 to $15 per ton. If, however, our farmers did not have the money or could not get credit to buy the hay, they had to shoot their stock or dispose of it in some other way at a very low price. The result was disastrous to many of our people. Again, in 1937, our farmers in many sections had a complete failure in grain and root crops. We did hav'' however, an abundant hay crop and this, added to a heavy carry-over from the previous year, gave us a large surplus for which there is no market. In fact there was a good deal of hay not harvested last year, and if we get a reasonable crop this year much of it will be left standing. We therefore now have this situation: in the maritimes a surplus of hay and a lack of seed grain and other mill feeds; in the west a lack of hay with seed grain and other mill feeds available for the maritimes if they pay for them. The government were aware of this situation last summer and also aware of the fact that the maritimes purchase large quantities of feed from the west at all times, and they should have, in the interests of the farmers of the maritime provinces, arranged for a sufficient reduction in the freight rates to enable the governments of the western provinces to purchase at least a portion of their hay requirements from the maritime provinces.
Since we are not allowed to load coal in grain cars, most of these must go back empty, and I submit that the railways, or at least the Canadian National, could have reduced rates on hay by two-thirds and still have done better financially than hauling back empty cars. Further, from the viewpoint and in the interest of the Canadian taxpayer it would have been far better business to handle the hay situation in this way and make work for Canadian railways, mines and farmers than to buy in Minnesota and send the Canadian taxpayers' money to the United States. I feel that in the interests of a united Canada this should have been done even at the cost of an increased outlay on the part of the government.

Seed Grain

I suppose that the hay requirements for the year are nearly filled, but I would strongly urge on the government the advisability of helping the maritime situation as far as possible, if only to the extent of having seed and feed grain cars for the next month loaded with hay for the return trip. I trust that it is not too late for some adjustment, but prompt action will be necessary, for it is now towards the end of March.
The sap is flowing from the maple trees on the Nova Scotia hills, and whether they obtain assistance or not, the maritime provinces will still carry on. If our farmers have not been able to obtain work during the winter to pay for their feed and seed grain they will sell some of their stock and the feed and seed from the west will continue to be paid for in hard cash. However, we are proud that the credit of our provinces continues to stand high and that a dollar is still a dollar and something that must be worked for and not obtained for the asking; that a debt is something to be paid.
Heading further west: when it is spring time in the Rockies and the cattle are on the ranges, as the federal treasury is standing the strain, all will be well on the western plain.

speechtext: Before the bill goes to the committee I wish to make one or two remarks. I should like to see the answers to those questions a little more fully developed as we go into committee on the bill. I asked first of all if the government considered that the amount of $14,500,000 was sufficient to guarantee seed to the farmers in the drought area. The Minister of Agriculture answered to the effect that we had had the same discussion last year; that everybody seemed satisfied with the amount that had been voted, and that there had been no complaints. I think that is true, but it is also true that there was no crop, and that by the third week of June it was quite apparent we were not going to have any crop.

Had there been a crop, and had farmers seen wheat going to the elevators for a good price at a time when they were not able to harvest very much, there would have been a great many complaints. Merely to say that there were no complaints last year hardly answers the question whether we are providing enough

money to supply sufficient seed to enable these people to sow at least an average crop this year.
As I said the other day, the basis on which we are distributing the seed is not fair to the man who is farming on a large scale. Last year the provincial government had what I regard as an excellent arrangement, and I wish that at this late date the government would consider following something of that sort rather than the plan outlined by the minister the other day. According to the forms sent out by the provincial government on January 28, 1937, if a man had a total of 160 acres ready for cultivation he received seed for three-quarters, or 120 acres; from 160 to 300 acres it was two-thirds, or 200 acres; from 300 to 400 it was three-fifths, or 240 acres; and over 400 acres there was a maximum of 300 acres. On seeding rates the basis was as follows: wheat, one to one and a quarter bushels per acre; oats, one and three-quarter bushels; barley, one and a half bushels; flax, half a bushel. The estimated amount of fuel was to be one and a half gallons of distillate per acre; six gallons of gasoline per hundred gallons of distillate; lubricating oil, four gallons per hundred gallons of distillate, and so on.
That was a much fairer basis on which to work out the distribution. According to the plan now proposed, the man who anticipates putting in 200 or 250 acres will get seed for 100 per cent of the land he has prepared, and the man with a large farm, let us say 1,000 acres, and there are many such, will get 250.

I submit that we ought to have some more information with reference to price. I was surprised the other day when the Minister of Finance said that the price would be between $1.40 and $1.45 a bushel. In my opinion, that is exorbitant to say the least. Much of that wheat was shipped out of the very districts into which it is going to be shipped this spring. I saw grain being shipped late in June and early in July last year from Creelman, Fillmore and other centres, and into these same districts wheat will have to be brought back for seed and the farmer will be asked to pay the freight both ways. It is a very unsatisfactory arrangement in view of the fact that we have known for a long time that seed would be required. Seeing that we have a wheat board it seems to me not inconceivable that we might have entered into an arrangement whereby the government would have been willing to work on a bushel for bushel basis, so that the farmer would sign, not for any specific amount of money but for the delivery of a number of bushels. He would have been able to deliver a bushel back for every bushel he had received and if there were handling charges in addition they could have been paid in cash. That would be a fairer basis, in my opinion. As it is, the farmer sold his wheat at a low price and now he gets it at a high price; and when he is ready to sell again the price will probably be low once more. I do not think it would be unfair to put the distribution on a bushel for bushel basis.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES

I wish to deal with one or two of the questions raised by previous speakers, and first I should like to deal with the point raised by the hon. member for Colehester-Hants (Mr. Purdy), who spoke a few moments ago, because he brought up a matter which I think is very pertinent to the discussion that has been taking place.
As has been pointed out, the financing of seed grain in western Canada is assisted under arrangements made by legislation passed by this house. There have been requests from other parts of Canada for similar assistance. We have had very insistent requests from those representing the provinces of Quebec, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, and some representations have been received from the province of Ontario with regard to the necessity for assistance in furnishing seed supplies. The government has taken the same position with regard to all these applications, and it is the position that was outlined the other evening when we were discussing this matter. The government has taken the position that where a municipality

Seed Grain
is able, because of its financial circumstances, to provide for the needs of those living in the municipality, then it is a local responsibility. Where the requirements are too great to be taken care of by the municipal organization the matter is referred to the provincial government; and where the provincial government intimates to the federal government that the problem is so great that it cannot be taken care of due to the financial condition of the province, then the federal government has always been prepared to examine into the conditions existing and arrive at a conclusion as to whether those representations were based upon the actual facts and whether under the circumstances we should take any part in assisting in providing seed.
I speak now only of ordinary seed requirements. In all the provinces of Canada we do give help in securing and providing registered seed to people who are using such seed in different parts of the country. We also give assistance to the governments of the various provinces in selecting seed in other parts of Canada, in order that it may be shipped to the provinces requiring it. But with regard to actual assistance in financing the purchase of seed itself, and other seeding activities within the province, we have never undertaken that as a federal government in any province, from anything I can find in the records, unless conditions were as I have outlined. That is, the municipality first declares itself unable to take care of the situation; the province then declares its inability to meet the need, so that the problem becomes a national one. Under these circumstances we have entered into the task of trying to assist in providing seed and seeding necessities. With that in mind we have always felt that so far as the federal government is concerned we could not undertake within any province, where drought had become so acute that the problem became a national one, to do anything that would necessitate our undertaking similar responsibilities in other provinces. We do not feel that it is the federal duty to undertake to assist in providing seed for those who are in a position to provide it for themselves.
Some of the suggestions .made this afternoon, if we were to accept them, might involve the government going so far as to assume responsibilities-both within the provinces where the drought is, and outside those provinces-that never have been anticipated in anything that has been done by this house, either under the present or under any previous government. As to whether or ntft the guarantee is sufficient, I can only repeat
what was stated the other evening. The present decision has been based upon the experiences of the past few years and we believe that the amount provided will be sufficient for what is assumed to be the federal government's responsibility in this matter, that is to assist the provincial government in providing the necessary financial assistance to put seed into the ground where it could not otherwise be obtained. Having decided that, we asked the governments of Saskatchewan and Alberta to provide us with information upon which to base our decision as to what the amount should be. As was indicated a moment ago by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas), the amount provided last year in Saskatchewan was $6,600,000. My memory is that the financial organizations did not undertake to go any further than the amount guaranteed by this government. They may have gone further, but in so far as this or the provincial governments were concerned, they did not undertake to go any further than the amount of the guarantee.

The legislation last year provided for a guarantee of $6,600,000. Some time in the month of July the government of Saskatchewan started to make representations with regard to seed grain. The first correspondence that we have on the files I believe is dated August 5. In reply to the questions asked by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) having to do with this particular matter, I can only say that the figure used in arriving at an estimate of the amount that would have to be guaranteed has been $1.45 per bushel. speechtext: The provincial government used the figure of $1.45. That figure was submitted to us as the outside cost and it was used in making our estimates of what the guarantee should be. My understanding is that it is the intention of the provincial government to charge the same rate for seed grain throughout the whole province. With regard to the size of the farms I can only say this: That is closely related to the matter I discussed first, namely, just how far a government should be expected to go in financing considerable acreage. That matter has been fully discussed by provincial governments, municipal bodies, individuals concerned, and representatives of the federal government for a great many years, and the conclusion arrived at is nearly always identical, or almost so, with the conclusion arrived at this year. Then on farms of over 320 acres of cultivated land they sow 50 per cent up to a maximum of 250 acres. The only difference

The other evening, when this matter was mentioned on two occasions, I purposely refrained from making any reference to it because, after all, as every hon. member now knows, the distribution of seed grain in western Canada, ever since seed grain was first distributed in the west, or at least ever since we have had municipalities in western Canada, has been handled largely through the municipal bodies. I am certain that that is true in Saskatchewan. No matter what government we have had in Saskatchewan, seed grain has been distributed through the municipal bodies.

Yes, and I am quite sure that members from western Canada will agree that there is no more non-partisan way in which seed grain could be distributed than through the municipal bodies, because, after all, in spite of what has been said in this house by members from time to time, every member from western Canada knows that our municipal elections out there, whether they be city, town or municipal, are seldom contested on any partisan political basis. Someone behind me says never, and I think that is probably a true statement of conditions existing there. Partisan politics do not enter into the election of councils in western Canada, and I say that on behalf of all parties so far as Saskatchewan is concerned. It is not the practice to allow either provincial or federal partisan considerations to enter into the election of councils.
I could bring into this house many communications that I have had, since this question became a matter of discussion, from municipal officials, some of whom have been strong supporters of members sitting on the opposite side of the house, indicating that at no time has the administration of relief or the distribution of feed and fodder or seed been made a matter of political consideration in Saskatchewan or in Alberta. I state that only to indicate that all of the political discussions I have ever heard with respect to this matter have taken place either in this house or in the legislatures of the provinces concerned. Political discussions in relation to the problem confronting us are taking place both in this house and in the legislatures of the provinces, and it is probably only natural that should be the case because there is no doubt whatever that elections, federal and provincial, do take place on a political basis. In so far as we on this side of the house, more particularly the ministers who are intimately concerned with the administration of matters of this kind, are concerned, we do not object in any way to any political discussions in the house with regard to this question or to any political accusations in regard to it, but we would like our friends who make political accusations to give us just a little more detail
Seed Grain

with regard to them in order that we might be able to answer them. With one exception I have yet to receive from a single municipality anywhere in Saskatchewan a statement to the effect that political considerations have been brought into the decisions in connection with these matters. That one municipality was in one of those districts which have been mentioned in some of the discussion to-day. When the matter was looked into, it was clearly shown that even in that case there had been no political considerations.
Dealing with the question of horses being brought back not in the best of condition, I can only say this: Again, it is not a matter of immediate federal consideration. But we have placed at the disposal of the provincial government of Saskatchewan the Carberry pasturage, which was referred to a few moments ago, composed of 130,000 acres of land which we fenced in last year in order to assist in handling the cattle that were being brought out of the drought area. We have also agreed with the Alberta government to make it possible for them to send horses to a ranch in the southern part of Alberta, and to pay the costs for the horses for both the pasturage in Alberta and the Carberry pasturage on a somewhat similar basis to what we would have paid had the horses been left at home.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: Which ranch is that?

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
It is a ranch in the
vicinity of Manyberries. The lease was being dropped this year by one of the ranchers who had been on it, and the pasturage has been used by the government to take care of some of these horses.
I am informed that the age of the horses in western Canada, more particularly in the drought area, is very much higher than it was when the drought period had its beginning, and that is only natural. People had been getting along with their old horses at a time when they had no funds with which to resupply themselves with younger horses, and according to our check, there were among the horses which went down to the Carberry pasture, at a time when some 1,500 had reached the pasture, about fifty that I would agree should never have been sent there. The check was not sufficiently careful to prevent old horses from being sent which could only die when they got there. It is just possible, too, that among those which were shipped back, some were too old to be able to rustle on the grass lands of that particular pasture and come through to the spring period in a proper condition to be placed upon the land in order to put in the crop. But what I wish to impress on the house is that that

is a matter which is being taken care of by the provincial governments. They have estimated all these things in coming to a conclusion as to how much money would be required, and I feel quite satisfied that, with the financial arrangement which is being made in both Saskatchewan and Alberta, the governments will be able to take care of the essential needs of those who require, first, seed, and, second, some form of assistance in connection with obtaining power to put the seed in the ground, and even to provide extra feed and fodder with which to put the work stock in shape to take care of seeding operations when they come.
It is now about a month away from the usual time of seeding a very considerable part of that area. The work stock is being returned to the area; the work stock in the area will be fed during the next two weeks or, in some instances, three weeks, out of feed and fodder that was provided through the winter months down to the end of March, and provision is made, under the legislation which is now going through, whereby that feed can be replenished out of the supplies of money that are being provided under this legislation to carry the stock through from the time when the winter supplies run out, to the end of the seeding period. Hon. members can rest assured that every consideration possible is being given to these matters, and also, I believe, that the municipalities in both provinces will take the same care this year as they have in past years to see that political motives do not enter into the consideration of this question. So far as I am concerned I have not heard that that was the case, either since this government has been in power or during the time the previous government was in office. There have been criticisms both when the previous government was in power and during the present government's term of office that too much consideration was given to political friends in the engaging of those who were employed from time to time to assist. But I believe that everyone, no matter to what political party he belongs, agrees that individuals once employed to take care of the situation existing in western Canada, whether they were municipal authorities or were directly engaged by governments, have not allowed party considerations to enter into the making of their decisions as to whether the man should, in the first place, have assistance, and in the second, how much he should get, and I am quite sure that that will not happen this year any more than it has happened in other years.

speechtext: With respect to the minister's statement that the cabinet and the inspector have the say as to the amount which shall be granted to a municipality, does he mean that the inspector will not examine each individual application which is made to the municipality and then report to the cabinet whether he approves it or not? Or does the inspector just take the question of the maximum amount granted to a municipality, and review that?

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: No; the provincial government does not do anything at all about the matter until the municipality makes application for seed assistance. If the municipality does not make application, the provincial government will not deal with the matter. When the municipal authorities make application, they include particulars of the acreage for which they desire assistance, the amount of seed they think should be provided for that acreage, the repairs they require, the amount of assistance for providing power; everything of that nature must be in the application. All that the government says is: "When we receive that application, we will not place it before one minister; we will appoint a committee of the council so that it will receive full consideration, and that committee will sit along with the inspector who has inspected the municipality and arrive at a conclusion as to whether their representations are justified by the actual facts." If they consider they are, that will be the amount allowed; jf they think it should be cut down, they will go back and discuss the matter with the municipality. That is the practice which has always been followed, and that practice, I am sure, will be followed this year.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
I do not propose at the _ moment to trespass upon the time of the house at any great length, but I should like to suggest that we treat this as an ordinary business transaction. We are asked on behalf of the Dominion of Canada to give our guarantee to the banks of this country to ensure them against loss for advances made to municipalities, which, in tu.rn, have been guaranteed by two of the western provinces. Ordinarily, if that were a business transaction submitted to any one of us, we should impose certain conditions upon the granting of our guarantee; if those conditions were absent, it would be regarded as bad business; if those conditions were present, it would be regarded as good business.
One of the matters which we have to consider is the price which the farmer has to pay
for what he gets. This perhaps is the most important of all the conditions with which we have to deal. By the use of some authority about which I shall speak when the house is in committee, this government utilized the wheat board for certain purposes. The statute says that the wheat board shall buy only from producers. The time when the wheat board extended its option to October is a matter of exact date. It had on hand a certain quantity of wheat. It was known that wheat would be required for seed in this country. Notwithstanding that fact the October option was extended. Then we proceeded to buy back that option.
That raises a question of first-rate importance in this country. It is one of the most important questions that will engage the attention of the house, because it is a large issue of principle which will have to be settled. The farmer is now called upon to pay on the basis of that option having been bought back and converted into cash wheat, and the price is mentioned as $1.45. Had the cash wheat been held before the option was extended to October, that difficulty would not have arisen. If any of us, dealing with this matter purely as a business transaction, had dealt with it in that way, we certainly should have had some difficulty with our shareholders. This is a matter in regard to which we require a good deal of explanation.
According to the papers which have been tabled, the wheat board remitted to the federal government eight million dollars, and deposited with this government two million dollars more, making a total of ten million dollars. That eight million dollars has gone into the revenues of the country. It represented profits which accrued in the manner indicated in the auditors' reports. The other two million dollars have been paid back to the wheat board for the purpose of enabling it to acquire the wheat on conversion of those options into cash wheat. In fact, the last report indicates that, in addition, the wheat board borrowed substantial sums from the banks of the country. Substantial loans have been made from banks. Under what authority? I can remember when authority was the all-important question on this side of the house, and when hours and days were taken up in discussing that question. But where is the authority to use the wheat board in the manner in which it has been used? An order in council has been read by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley); but the wheat board act provides only one thing, namely, that wheat shall be bought from the
Seed Grain

producer and no one else; and the price to be paid for it was 87| cents, and that only when the price of wheat reached 90 cents.
There are the facts; and yet the government has utilized the machinery of this statute without permitting the farmer to exercise his right to sell to the board, depriving him by the terms of an order in council which is illegal, without any question, because no condition which nullifies the operation of a statute can be imposed by order in council. That does not require argument even in this parliament; even the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bothwell) will not question that. No condition can be imposed upon a grant when it nullifies the statute under which it is granted. That is so simple that I should not even state it here. Those are the facts, and I submit that we must have adequate information with respect to that matter because it is the fundamental consideration in connection with this transaction.
In the second place, there is a good deal of force in the arguments that have been advanced this afternoon with respect to the acreage which is to be placed under crop. Not for a moment do I fail to recognize the difficulty of this government or of any government similarly situated. It has a right to impose conditions, because it is on our credit that this seed is being obtained. The conditions that it proposes to accept and not to impose are those found in an act of the Saskatchewan legislature. They have seen fit to provide that every person, rich or poor, high or low, who is so situated as to require assistance-not that they once did not require it, but they are now so situated as to stand in need of it-shall receive assistance only to the extent of 250 acres for seeding purposes. Well, I have lived in the west for forty years, and I have seen a quarter section, 160 acres, develop and expand and grow, until I have known a great many farms of a section, where it would not be unusual to expect 400 acres to be available, ready for seeding. I think I am stating the case fairly to those who know more about the matter than I do. There have been farms of a section and a half, of two sections, and of several sections. These people were once very well-to-do; all you have to do is to look at their places and see their houses, outbuildings, fences, and machinery. But by reason of the drought that we have now had upon us for more years than the evil days which fell upon Egypt, these people are practically penniless. It is a terrible thing to say, but I know men on relief in the west who were once very rich-well, not very 
rich, but more than comfortably off, quite well-to-do.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: And who still own quite a bit of land.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
Yes, men who still own land in the condition I have mentioned, land that has not produced any crop now for, in some instances, eight long years. One gentleman told me the other day that last year was the eighth year in which his crop had been destroyed by drought.
Are we doing right in limiting these people to 250 acres? I am not speaking in any partisan sense; I am merely stating my own observations and my own experience in dealing with these problems, and, mark you, I am not forgetting for a moment the fierce tirade of abuse levelled at us after the last world wheat congress when it was suggested that there might be a limitation in production. That suggestion was met with very fierce denunciation; yet that limitation is now to take place, and it is to be brought about when, if we may judge from the remarks of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) -and he has experience as a western farmer

 the moisture situation is favourable. The day before yesterday I was talking to a gentleman from the west and he went as far as to say this:	"I have been over the western
country these last few weeks, and I would regard the significant signs as being favourable to a crop in 1938." Of course, I am not unmindful of the fact that so many hon. gentlemen opposite, when parliament prorogued last year, were quite hopeful and, in fact, almost convinced that there would be a crop; yet we all know what the result has been.
Well, are we quite fair in giving this guaran- ' tee and accepting the limitation to 250 acres?
I fully appreciate the argument of the Minister of Agriculture a moment ago that there are corporations and mortgage and loan companies which will make loans. I say to the minister, however, that last year they did not make loans for seed grain. They advanced money and had the farmer buy seed, because he was working for them on a crop payment plan, so that if he got anything they got something, and if he got nothing they got nothing.
In the drought area a great many farmers got nothing, with the result that the advance had to be written off against profit and loss. What the minister says is quite clear. Some of these organizations will advance money to those who now occupy the position of tenant with them by reason of (a) foreclosure, under which they continue as tenants, or (b) pending final order of foreclosure, where they undertake to stay on, the understanding being that

Seed Grain
if they get a crop they will have something which will enable them to make the place their home again.

I had thought that class
was now merged with the class which had taken advantage to a considerable extent of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. My own observation, in those communities with which I have made myself familiar leads me to say with great frankness that the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act has been used by a very large number of those who found themselves with a mortgage bearing such a relation to present value that it was idle to think of being able to pay the mortgage off. But that is a matter of detail which need not enter into a discussion of the broad principle which I assert should be considered. I should like the government to consider whether it is not desirable to state as we have a right to do, as one of our conditions in giving this guarantee, that it might be made available for the acquisition of seed for a larger area than 250 acres. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) asked the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Dougles) a very pertinent question. He asked him, "What would you suggest?" He suggested a sliding scale. speechtext: Quite. One appreciates the attitude of the provinces. I think there is much in what has been said by both ministers, that the provinces should be better able than we are to determine the extent to which they will permit their people to incur obligations. On the other hand, the creation of new wealth is a matter of vital importance to Canada. It does not concern Saskatchewan and Alberta alone; it touches Ontario and British Columbia and every other part of this country. My only doubt has been as to whether we are shutting our eyes to the fact that there are very large farms in the west. I doubt not that the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) is cultivating now close to 1,000 acres of land.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES

The hon. member for Moose Jaw was finding a little fault because one hon. member used the word " cultivated." That is the language of the statute of Saskatchewan. The Minister of Agriculture is not wholly right in what he said as to distribution of seed grain in western Canada, because it will be remembered that the distribution of seed grain in western Canada commenced in the time when the present provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta were territories. It was then felt to be an obligation of the federal government, for they were administered under dominion control, and no question such as that raised this afternoon was raised.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
But I am pointing out the circumstances under which the first distributions took place. It was in the territories. I can recall how strange it seemed to me, coming from the east, to hear them talking about Ottawa distributing seed grain to the farmers of the country. Then I learned that the dominion government had taken the attitude that the people there were wards, using the word in a broad sense, provincial institutions not having been created. Notwithstanding the setting up of the provinces, it still became essential to advance money for seed grain, but this was done by the provinces making application to the dominion for assistance. Ever since the provinces were created in 1905, the method of distribution has not always been uniform. There have been times when one method was followed and other times when other methods were followed. But broadly and generally in Saskatchewan the matter has been left to the councils. Alberta was slower in developing

municipal government, except through what were called large improvement districts, and in those cases distribution was sometimes made through someone connected with the Department of Agriculture, who was permanently on the ground, or by a combination of several methods.
I suppose every hon. member knows what our unfortunate history about seed grain has been. In every ease we took a lien. It was a lien that attached by reason of a statute passed here. And from the day I first came into this house until I was endeavouring to administer the affairs of the country, the question was: How are you going to write off the seed liens?

speechtext: A former Minister of the Interior, Hon. Charles Stewart, was responsible, I think, for the last legislation in that regard. We had a sort of tribunal set up that dealt with these matters, and we used to pass orders in council on representations from this board, wiping out liabilities, or accepting smaller sums for larger, and thus getting rid of the liens. The hon. member for Colchester-Hants (Mr. Purdy) suggested that the dominion was going to lose this money. I do not share that view. If we get a crop, the province will be paid and we shall be paid.
