speechtext:
When the house rose at six o'clock we were discussing the seed and grain relief question. The members from the maritime provinces, Quebec, Ontario and British Columbia who have spoken on this subject should consider themselves fortunate in not having a condition such as this to face in their home districts. We are certainly sorry that we must ask for a government guarantee in Alberta for seed relief purposes. I have had it said to me on different occasions that the western members inadvertently give the western provinces a bad name by advertising them in the wrong way. The people in the east and other parts of Canada think that western Canada is impoverished and in a bad condition financially, socially and otherwise. I should like to disabuse the minds of hon. members of that notion by quoting the production figures for last year. Alberta produced 74,000,000 bushels of wheat, almost half the total production of Canada and more than half the total production of the western provinces. We produced 77,000,000 bushels of oats, and we produced practically half of the total barley produced in western Canada.
These figures show that all of Alberta has not been dried out. It is estimated that the 1938 wheat acreage in Alberta will be approximately 8,000,000 acres, while the acreage in Saskatchewan will be 13,000,000 acres. The wheat acreage in Saskatchewan is practically

all in the dried-out belt, while a large portion of the Alberta acreage is in a more humid region. At least 5,000,000 acres of the finest wheat land in Canada are in Alberta in sections that have sufficient moisture and rainfall almost to guarantee a crop. Any effort made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to diversify farming in Alberta and other parts of Canada will be appreciated by all of us. We would be more than happy to be able to produce large quantities of wheat even though we know that when that wheat is placed on the markets of the world, prices will naturally fall.
If we are to have a strong dominion, no part or province of that dominion must be discriminated against unduly. If business is to be good in one province, it must be good in all. As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) said, I think last year, it is no use to take from some of us to give to all of us. I want the people of eastern Canada to understand that this is merely a loan to the municipalities so that this part of Canada may be able to produce wealth more abundantly This is the first opportunity I have had of tendering my personal thanks to the people in the east for the vegetables, fruit and other materials sent to the impoverished farmers in my province.
Last year the government purchased a certain number of wheat options, and it would seem that they should have made some money on the transaction. On July 31, 1937, unsold wheat amounted to 6,964,000 bushels represented by futures contracts which, in the ordinary course of business, would have been disposed of prior to that date. I take these figures from the report of the Canadian wheat board. If any criticism is to come from me, it is that we should deplore this buying of options by the government. The farmers of western Canada have suffered greatly in the past because of attempts they have made to go into this business of buying options. Thousands of farmers have lost their all on the grain exchange at Winnipeg through buying and selling options. The options bought and sold on that exchange represent millions of bushels more than the actual crop raised.
I should like to illustrate my point by detailing what happened last summer on the grain exchange. The farmers of western Canada sold rye options for July delivery all the way from $1 to $1.40 a bushel. On July 31, 1937, rye was taken off the board at around $1.63 a bushel, while at the same time July wheat was $1.43. Many farmers thought it would prove profitable to sell rye and buy wheat, but in doing this they were playing

Seed Grain
into the hands of those who deal in this type of transaction. The result was that they were trimmed and certainly needed the apples which were sent out from the east.
Many of these men sold rye in the belief that if wheat went down, rye would also go down. But, lo and behold, when wheat went down rye went up! When the rye option was finally taken off the Winnipeg board, it was $1.63; wheat was $1.45 while cash rye was around 93 cents. The cash price was 70 cents a bushel below the paper price which was just a pen-and-ink quotation which could be wiped off the books at a single stroke. This is what was done, and thousands of farmers who had sold rye were deprived of their margin. I went into one office and asked them if they would take rye for these options. They told me that cash rye was 95 cents at that time. That meant that if we threshed our rye we would get only 90 cents a bushel, while the paper price was $1.63. I asked them what would happen if we imported rye from the United States. There was plenty of rye available in that country at 78 cents a bushel, but they told me that the United States rye was not as good as the Canadian. They always have some way of getting out of a thing like this. They wanted to take that rye off the books so that they could tell the men who held options that they had lost their money when July 31 came around. It was upon this subject that I had intended to say a few words before six o'clock.
In travelling through western Canada I find many farmers who have been stung at some time or another by the grain exchange. We are anxiously waiting for the report of the Turgeon commission and would like to know why it has not been brought down. We realize that something must be done to prevent manipulation in grain futures on the Winnipeg grain exchange and we deplore the government's participation in transactions of this kind. We believe that the government should have made money as a brokerage at one-thirty-second of a cent should be enough. If they were buying wheat in 1935 at around 89 cents a bushel, they should be making plenty of money when they sell it to the farmer at $1.45 a bushel. As a matter of fact, we feel that the farmer is entitled to wheat at a lower price than $1.45 a bushel for his seed in the drought areas. I know that cuts both ways, because in my own constituency there is a considerable amount of seed wheat for sale and we naturally want to see a good price for those who have it for sale. At the same time I would bring to
the attention of hon. members the disintegrating force that is exerted by such transactions as I have mentioned on the Winnipeg grain exchange, and which are dividing Canada instead of unifying it. Some hon. members wonder why the people of the west return men who are opposed to the present financial set-up, but it is really because we are being impoverished, more or less, by market manipulators not only in the west but also in the east.

The one. is with regard to the authority under which the wheat board was empowered to make these purchases of cash wheat; the other was with regard to the price per bushel which shall be paid by the Saskatchewan government for the wheat.
With regard to the authority, I have already given the explanation. The wheat committee of the cabinet met and decided that the chairman of the wheat board should be empowered to purchase this wheat, to turn the futures into cash wheat and supply the Saskatchewan government, and later the Alberta government as well. We did not think it was necessary to have an order in council. I am inclined to think we had the opinion of the solicitors of the Department of Justice; I am not quite sure about that, but I believe we were told that an order in council was not necessary to enable us to do this. I then wrote or telegraphed to the chairman of the wheat board that he could proceed in the direction indicated, namely the making of purchases of wheat and turning them over to the Saskatchewan government. Later on, as I said before-I think it was on the suggestion of Mr. Mclvor-it was thought that it might be better to have an order in council, conveying the authority in that way rather than merely by instructions from myself, authorized by the committee of the cabinet which has to do with wheat board matters. Having regard to the experience of some of us on this side with respect to this matter, I remember that it was always thought desirable to have some legal background for any action taken, and I find that the powers of the board, as defined by the statute, were:
(a)	to fix a price to he paid to the producer for wheat delivered to the board as by this act provided, subject to the approval of the governor in council;
(b)	to sell and dispose of from time to time all wheat which the board may acquire, for such price as it may consider reasonable, with the object of promoting the sale and use of Canadian wheat in world markets;-
Those were the days when the advertisements with respect to bread were running so prolifically in British papers. I am quoting from section 8 of chapter 53 of the statutes of 1935:
(e) to sell and dispose of stocks of wheat and contracts for the delivery of wheat acquired from Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited and the wheat represented by such contracts as may be reasonably possible, having regard to economic and other conditions.

He did not. He dealt with it as defined in this statute:
(i) in selling and disposing of wheat as by this act provided, to utilize and employ without discrimination such marketing agencies, including commission merchants, brokers, elevator men, exporters and other persons engaged in or operating facilities for the selling and handling of wheat, as the board in its discretion may determine;-
In other words, the existing machinery was to be used; options were given and taken, and everything else was provided for.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: But McFarland bought 14,000,000 bushels of futures.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
Absolutely, under that
section, and bought them for the board.

speechtext: Without any authority whatever.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: No; it was bought by the old cooperative before the board came into being, while it was still awaiting the authorization of the governor in council with respect to matters such as price and so on. But do not let us get away from the main issue, which is, by what authority this board, under the direction of the government, is now undertaking to give, in consequence of that arrangement, a guarantee which means that it will cost the settlers and farmers of Saskatchewan something in the vicinity of $1.45 a bushel for their wheat.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: If they had bought it in any other way, would they have bought it for any less?	*

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: The board were not buying wheat. They had their options and said they were going to take delivery of the wheat. That is not buying wheat. The other man had to go out and buy it and give it to the board.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: One or two more observations like that and the hon. member for Waterloo North will cry for " Blucher or night." That more nearly proves what we are saying than any observations which have been made by the minister. It is quite true that the board had become sellers of wheat, and they became sellers to Saskatchewan. They must be sellers at a price because the statute says they cannot sell except at a price. We want to know at what price they sold and that is what we have asked for. In view of the fact that the government directed the board to do this, surely we have the right to know three and a half months afterwards at what price they sold.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
I have told that to my right hon. friend.
Seed Grain

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: Would the minister with his generous disposition that he sometimes masks behind a frowning countenance be good enough to explain just what was the price?

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: I would be merely repeating what I have said already, and I am not going to burden the committee by doing that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: My right hon. friend with his usual great ability has succeeded in weaving apparent mystery around a perfectly simple transaction. Here we had a condition in western Canada; it became apparent in June and July that over that great area there would not be a sufficiency of good seed for the following year. At the same time there existed a government agency, the wheat board, which had in its possession just short of 7,000.000 bushels in wheat futures contracts. These were just the same contracts as they had taken over originally from what my right hon. friend describes as the McFarland board. These futures contracts for wheat entitled the holder to get delivery at Fort William.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: They could deliver No. 1, No. 2, No. 3 or No. 4 northern, or No. 1 or No. 2 garnet.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: I shall come to that in a moment. What would have been said of this government if, with a government agency holding nearly 7,000.000 bushels in wheat contracts, wheat had nevertheless been allowed to go out of the country and the farmers had been consequently unable to sow their land? As I recall it, we looked at the situation in late July after we came back from the imperial conference. I am glad my right hon. friend admitted a few moments ago that the wheat board had a perfect right to turn these futures contracts into real wheat, because that is the point.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: They have to sell wheat. The law says that is their job.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
If the wheat board had the power under the statute to turn its futures contracts into cash wheat at any time, then there can be no question about the authority of the wheat board to go through with this transaction which we are discussing. Why is that? Once it has authority to turn futures contracts into real wheat, can there be any doubt as to its authority to keep that real wheat? Goodness knows, the wheat boards and the authorities which preceded them did keep wheat and wheat futures contracts for long enough periods, and they must have had authority to do so. At least, I am giving my right hon. friend credit for believing 
that he had authority to do what he did, just as we believe that we have authority to do what was done in this case.
What do we find? We find the wheat board as a matter of national interest instructed by a committee of the cabinet that, in view of the shortage of good seed, it would be better not to let wheat get out of the country so that we would be short of seed. Proceeding steadily from August on, the board proceeded to convert these futures contracts into actual wheat. It is apparent that it would have been useless and wasteful for them to have taken delivery of that wheat at Fort William, because Fort William is not the place where the wheat is required for seed. In addition, there would be heavy freight charges in shipping the wheat westward from Fort William to the places at which it was required. An even more important matter is that the deliverer of wheat under a futures contract would, as my right hon. friend well knows, have the power to tender to the board No. 1, No. 2, No. 3 or No. 4 northern. These futures contracts permit the deliverer to deliver these lower grades of wheat at an agreed upon discount.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
And No. 1 and
No. 2 garnet.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
All the garnet mixtures
could have been delivered. I shall do my right hon. friend the justice of saying that he never suggested that they should take delivery at Fort William.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: He certainly did not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: He knows perfectly well that if the holder of the futures contract does not elect to take delivery at Fort William under the terms of the contract, and requires delivery at some other place, he must negotiate the terms upon which that delivery is to be made, because it is a departure from the original contract which involves the possible delivery, as I have stated, of No. 1, No. 2, No. 3, or No. 4 northern at Fort William. I submit that not only had the wheat board a perfect right under this statute, as stated by my right hon. friend, to do everything which has been done thus far, but it had the undoubted power, as he says, to turn these futures contracts into cash wheat.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: No; I did not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
It had the undoubted
power to acquire that cash wheat, and it has the undoubted power to sell that cash wheat to the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta in order that the farmers may sow it during the spring of 1938. The transaction

Seed Grain
is a perfectly simple one. As my right hon. friend says, they are sellers of wheat; their business is to sell wheat. Therefore, it is not their business to sell below the market. I believe I am correct in saying that the adjustments will involve turning the wheat over to the provinces concerned, to Saskatchewan at any rate, at a price based upon the average of prices between July 31 and whatever date is arranged for as the delivery date after this legislation has passed and it is possible to put through the financial aspects. My right hon. friend may take the financial statement and say that the surplus which existed now becomes a debt to the bank, and so on. He knows how simple that really is.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
Certainly it is.
Mr. DUNNING; It does not cost all these amounts to carry wheat futures, but it does cost something to carry real wheat. Interest must be paid; storage charges must be paid, and freight charges must be paid when the wheat is moved from one place to another. The freight charges to each of the 1,100 individual destinations within the province of Saskatchewan will have to be paid. If, after that has been done, the prices involved are to be based upon the averages such as I have indicated, who can say that the transaction is an unfair one from the standpoint of the board, on the one hand, and from the standpoint of the farmers who are getting the seed, on the other?
The provincial governments appear to be perfectly satisfied. They are the primary debtors in the matter, and they have examined the whole transaction. They have dealt with the wheat board; they have not dealt with the government. The wheat board has perfect authority under this statute to sell wheat. In making arrangements to sell to these provinces, I submit that it is acting as much within its power as though it were selling to a miller, to an exporter or to any one else who might be buying wheat. There is the simplicity of this whole transaction. There is nothing mysterious about it at all.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
If these orders in council are correct, there is a distinct limitation on the part of the wheat board with respect to this wheat. This is not the wheat that is covered by a special section in chapter 53 of the statutes of 1935. Paragraph (c) of section 8 reads as follows:
(e) to sell and dispose of stocks of wheat and contracts for delivery of wheat acquired from Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited and the wheat represented by such contracts-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
Yes-"and the wheat
represented by such contracts."

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
Surely. It goes on:

as may be reasonably possible, having regard to economic and other conditions.
That is what they had to sell. Then there is another provision with regard to their getting the wheat. That wheat, we find by the government's own records, was purchased by Saskatchewan, and here is why I say that- and, mark you, before any conversion took place at all-Saskatchewan bought the wheat under the provisions of that subsection.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: It is not bought yet.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
All right; then I am going to ask this question: Why did you pass the order in council on the fifteenth of December?
The committee of the privy council had before them a report, dated 13th December, 1937, from the Minister of Trade and Commerce, stating that the Canadian wheat board advise with regard to the question of converting wheat futures into actual wheat to be used for seed and feed relief in the province of Saskatchewan, that arrangements have been made by the Saskatchewan government for the purchase of this wheat.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: Exactly-"arrangements"; and they are not completed yet.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: Surely the hon. gentleman knows that the arrangements are arrangements to purchase the wheat; but being the kind of lawyer that he showed himself this afternoon, perhaps he has not appreciated that fact.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: Not a lawyer; but we have the wheat.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
This order in council says that they arranged to purchase the wheat, and here is the amazing part of it:
-and that all charges in connection with the handling, such as premiums, storage, transportation and any additional charges will be paid by the Saskatchewan government.
So that on December 13 last the government knew that the wheat board had sold the wheat to Saskatchewan.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: We knew it before that.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: Surely. The Minister of Finance said he knew it when he came back from England, and I assume that the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who does not seem to have graced that occasion with his presence, knew of it during the absence of the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Trade and Commerce had been wandering around Australia-

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
So had the right hon. gentleman.
Seed Grain

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: -and he learned during the absence of the Minister of Finance what was the fact. Here are the transactions. First, the wheat board, as authorized by law, sold wheat futures to the government of Saskatchewan.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: Not futures; they sold wheat.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
But the law says they have the right to sell wheat:

and the wheat represented by such contracts as may be reasonably possible, having regard to economic and other conditions.
They sold the wheat and they undertook to convert the futures into real wheat for the government of Saskatchewan. I want to know where their authority to do it came from.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman himself said they had authority.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: The hon. gentleman misunderstood that observation. That had reference to their duties with respect to sales. They had no right to do a job for the province of Saskatchewan and take the risk of this money being paid.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: Take the risk of its being paid?

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: Yes, by Saskatchewan, the premiums and all the handling charges.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: There was the same risk if they sold it to anybody else.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: May I ask the right hon. gentleman what act he is quoting from?

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: The Canadian Wheat Board Act of 1935, section 8, paragraph (c), and I have been reading from the order in council passed on the fifteenth day of December, 1937, which undertook to authorize something to be done which, according to the auditor's report, had already been done on a large scale, and for which the wheat board made an arrangement with the province of Saskatchewan as a corporation. It may have had power to contract to do a job of work for the province of Saskatchewan, but it is not so indicated in the powers granted to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: Read section 7.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
Section 7 provides:
The board shall undertake the marketing of wheat in interprovincial and export trade and for such purposes shall have all the powers of a corporation and without limitation upon such powers the following

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
"Without limitation," it says.
[Mr. Euler 1

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES

There is a special clause that dealt with the cooperative wheat, and then you find in paragraph (c) of section 8 that the general powers of this board were entirely different from its powers with respect to this particular wheat. That wheat formed the subject of special legislation. It was discussed in committee and there were varying views about it. Hon. members will remember the difficulties that came about with regard to the acquisition of this wheat. There is no question how that difficulty came about, is there? Paragraph (f) of section 7 says:
Notwithstanding anything hereinbefore contained, to acquire from Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited, upon terms to be approved by the governor in council, all wheat or contracts to purchase or take delivery of wheat in respect of which the government of Canada has given a guarantee.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: Does my right hon. friend interpret the words in section 8, "it shall be the duty of the board," to constitute a limitation on the general powers that he read a moment ago in section 7 giving the board the powers of a corporation?

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: The duty of the board legally imposed on them the obligation-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: Does that limit the general powers given under section 7?

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: Paragraph (c) dealt specifically with the board's wheat. The cooperative wheat was dealt with. After we get it into their possession, there is a definite way in which it has to be treated. It stands separately. There were no participation certificates to be given with respect to that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: But the very language of paragraph (c) permits everything that one could desire.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
Paragraph (c) puts a limitation on this wheat as distinguished from any other. I am not stickling over technicalities. The board undertook this work for Saskatchewan. What I am coming to is this: We knew what the situation was prior to the end of July. We had some clear appreciation of it apparently towards the beginning or middle of July at any rate. We did not do anything, but Saskatchewan did. We then permitted them to acquire the wheat; but we did not pass any order in council until they wanted to purchase some seven million bushels of wheat, and we passed an order in council in December authorizing them to do it in August, that is-after it had all been done.

Seed Grain
Then comes the question what the price is to be. The statute is obligatory on the price.
I do not know yet what the price was. I have been trying to find out all night. I am tremendously interested in the price, as every member is, because it affects two things. First, it affects the standing of the wheat board with respect to the McFarland wheat. Second, it affects the price the farmers of western Canada are going to pay for that same wheat. At what price was that wheat sold?

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: Before the minister answers, I understand that the right hon. gentleman says that he is quoting from sections of the 1935 Canadian Wheat Board Act, and he is endeavouring to find out what authority the government had under the act to purchase the wheat for the province of Saskatchewan. I happened to be on the wheat committee a year or so ago, and as I remember it, the board under Mr. McFarland purchased some ten million bushels of wheat, not for any provincial government, but by way of wheat options for the purpose of gambling on the wheat market at that time. These facts were brought out before the wheat committee; they have never been refuted by anyone; and surely, if Mr. McFarland had that power at that time under this act, the government should have the same power under this legislation to purchase wheat for the provincial government that needs to buy seed for the farmers in that province.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: I suppose it may be desirable to make it clear that that observation has no merit in fact. I, therefore, shall do so. It was the cooperative enterprise that bought the ten million bushels of wheat.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: With th% same gentleman acting as chairman or manager of the cooperative.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: It was not the wheat board that bought it. Supposing the hon. gentleman just retracts the false statement he made.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: What false statement?

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: That the wheat board bought ten million bushels.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: Mr. McFarland bought it.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: Mr. McFarland did not. The cooperative enterprise bought the wheat. We had the evidence of that. It was before the Turgeon commission.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: What Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde do is the same thing.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: Well, it may be that the hon. member feels that he has added to his reputation by making that observation. It is true they sold some wheat during the next few days; but whatever parcel was mixed with it, the general body of wheat was turned over to Mr. Murray, on which a profit-

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: It does not make any difference.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: The hon. member says it does not make any difference.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: Not a bit.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: The only difference I would suggest is that it would be the generous and kindly thing to say, " I made a mistake when I said that the wheat board bought the wheat. The cooperative bought it." It would sound better and look better in the future.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: The facts came out before the wheat committee. Mr. McFarland was working at the same time for both the wheat board and the cooperative under a guarantee from the government of this country.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES

speechtext: I wonder whether the right hon. leader of the opposition would tell us with whose money Mr. McFarland bought this twelve to fourteen million bushels?

Seed Grain

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: With a guarantee from the government of Canada.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: Is clause 2 carried?

If I remember rightly, the Saskatchewan government last year canvassed the different municipalities and asked them to give an estimate of how much seed would be needed and what the acreage would be, and on the basis of that survey the Saskatchewan government asked for a certain sum of money to be granted by the federal government. The amounts given by the Minister of Agriculture last year were: wheat,
2.739.000	acres; oats, 1,300,000 acres; barley,
39.000	acres; flax, 14,400 acres; rye, 10,400 acres, making a total of 4.102,800 acres for which seed was to be supplied. A survey had been made, and on the basis of that survey a definite amount was stipulated as required to satisfy the operations. Has anything like that been done this year? The minister said that he had no definite figures as to acreage; but both Alberta and Saskatchewan must have made some survey in order to find out what the requirements would be, and at least an approximate figure must have been arrived at of the number of acres to be seeded, so that we should have some idea of the total acreage as compared with the total acreage last year.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: Those who have been associated with the making of estimates in connection with seed grain and seed grain requirements in Saskatchewan, and in AJberta as well, have been working at this job, most of them, during the whole seven or eight years that there has been necessity for supplying seed to the people of those provinces, and the same type of officials here at Ottawa have been engaged during all that period in checking all those estimates. Some of the ministers here at the present time have also had previous experience of the same kind in the provinces. With all that experience we know fairly well what the acreages are likely to be, but no one is prepared to make more than an estimate of the situation at the present time.

speechtext: Not on a full acreage crop.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
There was slightly over two bushels to the acre grown altogether, and by the time you cleaned that and eliminated what was unfit for seed, there was not sufficient grown in the province last year to seed the province. Furthermore, what is generally spoken of in this house as the drought area is not the drought area at all. What has been spoken of as the drought area comprises 170 municipalities in Saskatchewan, for which the federal government pa>rs the full cost, and fifty-two municipalities in Alberta for which the federal government also bears the full cost in connection with relief. But in Saskatchewan that is not half of the area in the whole province which is suffering from drought this year. The new sections are not in exactly the same position as the other sections of the province, because much of the land is suffering now its first year of drought. Some of it had a year of drought in 1931 and no drought since, and to begin to estimate the requirements of those sections as against the requirements of the other sections, would be, I think, futile. I have all the yields in the different municipalities, and I could read them to the committee, but they would not be of any value. Municipality after municipality has no yield whatever. When you get into the neighbourhood of Qu'Appelle river and Long lake, coming from the southwest, you get from two to two and a half bushels, and in areas still further removed to the north and east you get around four and five, while at the very best in some limited areas you get seven, eight or nine bushels. But those areas are extremely limited.
To speak of wheat in Saskatchewan last fall which might have been kept for seed purposes is to overlook the fact that it would have cost more to have kept it in Saskatchewan and to have shipped it from where it was to where it is needed than to have purchased it in Alberta or in Manitoba and shipped it in. All these matters enter into the estimate of acreage, and the nearest estimate that can be made by any one at the moment is the estimate I gave this afternoon, namely, that there will be in the neighbourhood-it may be above or it may be below this figure-of 12,000,000 acres upon which seed will have to be put through government assistance. This does not mean that the whole 12,000,000 acres will be seeded to wheat, or that the whole 12,000,000 acres will receive seed from the governments. There is, however, an acreage of 12,000,000 acres that we shall have to consider giving assistance to. If we take TMr. Gardiner.]
Alberta, the regulations there permit of seeding up to 300 acres; but that includes all that the farmer has in his bin, and to estimate the acreage there for which seed will have to be supplied as compared with some other areas where the farmer cannot possibly have seed in his bin, is an impossibility and something that would not help the committee in arriving at a decision as to what should be done.
The whole acreage that requires assistance from the government will get assistance somewhat on the basis which has been outlined to the committee, a basis that, as I pointed out at the beginning of .the discussion this evening, was not properly set out in the statement made the other day and this afternoon again, to the effect that the acreage was set in legislation. The acreage is provided for through the regulations provided for in the legislation, and that is subject to some change. But that is an acreage set for the purpose of making an estimate, and anything that can be given the committee can be nothing better than an estimate. We are relying on the provincial and municipal governments to do this year as they have always done in their own interests, to hold the amount down to actual requirements but at the same time to see to it that the province and the municipality are not placed in a difficult position next fall, if they have a crop, in consequence of no seed having been put in the ground this year. They are as anxious to collect tax rates as we are to do the right thing by these people, and we are just as anxious to do the right thing by them as anyone in this committee can be. All that we think it necessary for this committee to do is to keep a proper check to see that money advanced by the people of Canada is not squandered, and to rely on the elected representatives of the people in the province and the municipalities to take care of the needs of the people so far as these total amounts permit of that being done. I think that, having made that check, we have done all that this committee should expect in connection with a matter of this kind.

enable the provinces to carry out the obligation they were assuming. This government felt sure that this parliament would, by this method, once more give those western plains a chance to grow a crop. Perhaps I could explain the way in which this is arrived at. It has been known in previous years, and particularly last year, about what the average cost would
be for the whole acreage to be seeded in a municipality, or even in a whole province for that matter. The percentage of the land worked with horses and the percentage worked with tractors are fairly well known to the government authorities in both provinces. They estimate that a certain percentage of the crop will be seeded with tractors which will require a certain amount of fuel. A particular farmer will need so many gallons of gasoline and so much oil because he is farming so many acres with a tractor. But to put that into either a regulation or a law would be placing the provincial governments and the municipalities in a much more difficult position than they would be in otherwise. We know this from experience. I think it is much better to make estimates of what the average cost per acre will be; what is the average requirement for repairs; what will be the average amount of oil and gasoline required to operate a tractor; what will be the average amount of feed and fodder required; I think it is much better to arrive at one's conclusions and to set the limits in that way.
Then we can allow those who are closer for purposes of administration to arrive at decisions as to what ought to be done. I am sure that the hon. member for Weyburn will agree that if it is impossible for a municipal council to make the decision, and make it properly, or impossible for an inspector on the ground, no matter how he may be appointed, to make it, it is impossible for us to do it here. You may criticize the methods of appointment of the inspectors and all that; but if the inspector is capable of checking a quarter section of land, and he walks over it and sees its condition and the equipment that is on it, he is in a much better position to state what the amount ought to be than any hon. member, no matter how familiar he may be with agriculture. The best we can do in connection with these matters is to set the maximum amount which can be used for different purposes; to try to get that maximum as near as we can to the actual requirements, based on experience; then to set up the best checking organization we can get and see that the best inspection system is set up, not by ourselves but by others, for we only check that work; and then try to see that none of the money provided is wasted. When we have done that, I think we have done practically all we can do, and I would hesitate to put my opinion either in the form of a regulation or in legislation of this parliament as to how much gasoline should be used to farm a quarter section of land.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: I am not deterred from doing what I conceive to be my duty by the criticism that I am not a farmer; I am dealing with legislation only as such. Might it not be desirable to incorporate in the statute the regulations that at the moment are purely regulations? Shortly put, the only protection we have here with respect to either of these provinces is the maximum of the amount we may guarantee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
It must be used for certain purposes.
Seed Grain

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: We are not going to have control of that. That is my whole point. You start with the municipality. The Minister of Agriculture has dwelt upon the desirability of including the municipality because of the knowledge they have of local conditions. But, while the Minister of Finance is the custodian of the country's money, the bald fact is that the amounts of $1,900,000 for Alberta and $14,500,000 for Saskatchewan constitute the only limitation imposed in connection with this whole matter. You can think it over as carefully as you may. I have been sitting here for the last fifteen minutes going over it as carefully as I can.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: The terms of the statute are fairly explicit.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: I know. But the provincial statute has been worked out by the people on the spot. What we thought of as a statute is purely regulation, and the government is introduced as one of the bodies that determine the matter, but as far as the Dominion of Canada and its taxpayers are concerned the only limitations imposed on our liability are those two amounts of $1,900,000 and $14,500,000. That is the reason why I started out with the idea that we should endeavour to impose some limitation in the way of conditions in the statute itself and make it a criminal offence to endeavour to violate it, because in communities there are rackets that arise which one little expects. I could give day and date with respect to some that have occurred in all parts of the country. We have them in every province; we all know that. All one has to do is to take the reports which come in sometimes from the mounted police, and one can find out without much difficulty what happens in some of these communities. No one for a moment questions the honesty of the great majority of the people. But when one is dealing with something which belongs to a government, the rule of conduct is not the same. I do not see sufficient safeguards in the legislation. However, I am not going to labour the matter further.

Section agreed to.
On section 4-Governor in council to approve form and terms of guarantees.

speechtext: Would the minister be good enough to repeat that figure-I have been looking through his statements of the other day and I do not find it-with respect to the total amount of guarantees over the seven or eight years during which the dominion government has made those guarantees.

Well, the guarantee

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
I shall give a brief statement with reference to it. In 1932-33 Manitoba got $600,000 by way of loan from the dominion government. Saskatchewan in the same year got $6,000,000 and Alberta, $140,000. In 1933-34-these are still loans to the governments, remember-Manitoba got for relief in the drought area, including seed grain, $250,000. There was nothing for Saskatchewan or Alberta in that year. In 1934-35 Manitoba got $225,000 for relief in the drought area, including seed grain; Saskatchewan got $3,000,000 for seed grain, and by way of specific loans to pay relief, feed and seed accounts on hand July 31, 1934, to 31st August, 1935, $4,500,000. Alberta in the same year got $2,095,000 for assistance in seed grain and seeding operations. In 1935-36 Manitoba received $408,000 under similar conditions to those previously related; Saskatchewan, $6,000,000, and Alberta, $1,100,000. The totals up ot that date, because that was the last year in which the direct loan policy was followed, are: Manitoba, less repayments, $1,106,000; Saskatchewan, less repayments, $18,900,000; and Alberta less repayments, $3,195,000.
It will be noted that some of these are not wholly for seed grain; there were years in which seed grain and relief were more or less run together. These amounts that I have indicated were, of course, affected to some degree by the write-offs authorized a year ago over loans generally in that year. But with respect to our guarantees which have been given, no losses have been paid by the dominion up to now. That is because the dominion's responsibility does not become enforceable until there have been three crops,

Seed Grain
including the crop sown, and that has not occurred as yet. Therefore, under the guarantees it cannot be said yet what our ultimate loss will be. It will be remembered that when I first suggested this type of legislation to the house two years ago, I related the satisfactory experience which Saskatchewan had had with the guarantee method as compared with the direct loan method over the years in the past. Where you have the guarantee method with the machinery of the municipality and of the bank helping you to collect, the experience during the years in which the credit of that province was good, when the province did not have to come to the dominion at all for supplementary credit, was that the great bulk of such seed grain loans were repaid under the guarantee method. Of course, we have not the conditions to deal with that have prevailed in 1936 and 1937.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
As I understand it, the
seed will be given through the municipalities, the province guaranteeing the municipality and the dominion guaranteeing the province, in this case to the banks, in an amount of some 814,500,000. What I want to know is why, in the matter of seed, the same principle is not followed as in connection with relief. In the distribution of relief the Minister of Labour does not deal with the municipalities. Why utilize a quasi-political body like the governor in council? Why not use Mr. Purvis, former head of the employment commission, who was selected by the Minister of Labour and was the representative of the duPont dynasty in Canada. The Globe and Mail is evidently trying to unload him on our party as leader so as to make our party, as it were, merely an adjunct of the duPont dynasty of America, and we are not going to become any such thing. I submit that there should be a principle behind every vote. Why should we deal differently with Saskatchewan and Alberta and let the farmers deal directly with the municipalities? Why should the Ontario government not deal directly with the mayors in relief matters, as in this Bill No. 78, instead of having the municipalities deal with and through the province? There is a principle involved, and I submit the proposed method is unfair. The same principle should apply in all the provinces on all relief measures.

speechtext:
I should like the minister
to look into the question of power. I think it would be advisable to discuss this matter with the provincial government, because there is no question about a shortage of power. I
have heard the statement made by the superintendent of one of the experimental farms in the west, that 40,000 horses which had been shipped to eastern Canada in the winter would not come back. That will deplete the horse power in the province to a considerable extent. The question is a serious one, and I hope the ministers will take it up with the provincial authorities and that more assistance will be given than is provided for under the legislation as it stands.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: In outlining the regulations the Minister of Agriculture said that a committee of the cabinet and an inspector for the district would determine the amount of seed grain to be advanced. Who will have the final veto? The municipal council will receive applications from a number of farmers and those applications will be forwarded to the committee who will sit in with the inspector from that particular district. If it is decided that the amount is too much, will the reduction be made on a percentage basis or will the individual applications be reviewed and reductions made where deemed advisable? The minister said that six men in a municipal council were in a better position to know the farmer's needs than we were in this house. I have heard that before, but often the municipal council's decision is vetoed by someone else. I know, of course, that there must be some control; but I should like to know where the veto will lie, and whether the final decision will cover the total advanced to the municipalities or whether individual cases will be considered.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
That is entirely a matter of provincial administration, and anything that I may say with regard to it cannot be at all conclusive. The practice is for farmers to apply to the secretary of the municipality, and when the council meets the applications are submitted and discussed by the committee who know the conditions. The applications are submitted either to the whole council or to a committee of the council and to the representative of the government, who will be this inspector spoken of here, and he reports back to Regina with regard to the matter. He makes his own check, and the decision is usually reached as a matter of agreement between the province and the municipality in exactly the same way as we reach an agreement with the provinces. They

discuss the matter from all points of view and decide upon the total amount to take care of the municipality.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: Will the inspector be the final authority on the question as to what a certain farmer shall have, or by what amount his allotment shall be cut down?

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: In 99 cases out of 100 they will agree that there is no final authority.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: Some of the councils do not feel that way.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: Why does the minister put paragraph (ii) in this form? We are dealing with our own guarantee, and I should have thought we would have said that we are not going to give a guarantee for any liability which accrues prior to three years from the date the guarantee is given to the province. The conditions under which our obligation attaches under the second sub-paragraph of section 5 make it referable entirely to the provinces. I should have thought the minister would have said that our guarantee should not become effective until three years after the date of the payment by the banks, because it is covered by the agreement. We introduce into this bill a provision that it does not prevent the province from making voluntary payments from time to time before the expiration of the three years. What have we to do with that? Obviously any money the provinces pay, so much the better for us. The whole fabric is based on a different appreciation of the transaction that I have. We, the federal power, are not concerned about their condition; all we should say would be that our guarantee would not attach until three years after the date in any event when the payments were made by the bank.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: I speak with bated breath about the part of section 5 to which my right hon. friend refers, because nothing has had more microscopic attention on the part of eminent legal counsel than this section, in order to ensure that the liability of the province and that of the government of Canada shall be separate and successive, and not joint-

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: That is clear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: -and, second, that we shall not give a dominion guarantee except in cases where the province has arranged that it shall have three years before its liability is enforced.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
That is where we differ.
[Mr. Gardiner !

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: With all respect I can only say that that is as I am advised.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: I do not want to question the law officers, but I have seen some fearful and wonderful products occasionally. This undoubtedly makes the province the determining factor. I refer particularly to that part which provides that the province shall not be prevented from making payments from time to time. What have we to do with that? All we have to say is the second condition, that no liability shall accrue under our guarantee until the expiration of three years from the date of the advance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: With deference I think my right hon. friend is missing one point, namely, that there is to be a provision forbidding me as Minister of Finance to sign a guarantee unless the guarantee given by the province has the three year leeway. My right hon. friend will see that if the government could be required by the banks to pay in advance of the expiry of the three year period, that would create an obligation which the dominion government, if not under the terms of this legislation, at least for the sake of the credit of the country, would have to meet. So we endeavour to take care of it by saying that the Minister of Finance must not give the guarantee of the dominion unless he is sure that the province which is being guaranteed will not be required by its creditor to pay until three years from the date of the advance. That is really the intention. Then, in order to provide for the possibility of the province paying sums voluntarily in advance of requirement, the exception is made. Of course we are very anxious to have them do that.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: I merely say that the minister has much greater confidence in the provinces when he is dealing with the distribution of seed and oil and feed than when they are making a bargain with the banks. If the provinces have not intelligence enough to make the bargain that you say they have to make before you will give your guarantee, I have not that measure of confidence as to the other things which have been said here tonight with respect to the distribution of seed, oil, etc., because the provinces have to make that bargain, not we.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: But we refuse to come in unless it is a particular kind of bargain.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: Well, this may be the way to do it.

speechtext: That is an extraordinary clause. Surely the Prime Minister was not present in council when this bill was passed. Look at what the governor in council is going to do. He is going to decide that Saskatchewan is unable to pay its debts.

speechtext: The colleague of my right hon. friend, the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, last year raised the point in connection with similar legislation to this in connection with the words in section 5, paragraph (i), "that the province is unable to fulfil its guarantee." He prophesied that such words would be completely unsatisfactory to the banks. He said there must be some means of defining when inability on the part of the province arises. We have tried to meet that point, because I may say the banks took the hint and did advance legal doubts as to the position. We have tried to meet the difficulty by section 7.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: I should say it makes it possible to attach an entirely different meaning to the words "inability to pay." The way in which it has been expressed is that the governor in council may by order, not define what is inability to pay, but define the circumstances under which the province shall be conclusively deemed unable to pay.
